voices.name: Jane Austen
voices.title: Jane Austen
voices.tagline: Irony, balanced periods, judgement in a word

epigraph.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.

moves.name: Clauses balanced in one period
moves.does: Clauses held in one sentence by “, and”, “; and”, “; but”, “, which”, the main point arriving late; a short sentence kept only for a turn or a verdict.

moves.name: Judgement in abstract nouns
moves.does: Feeling and character named by abstract nouns of judgement rather than things described: civility, propriety, composure, mortification, felicity, indifference, consequence, spirits.

moves.name: Understatement and litotes
moves.does: The verdict implied by understatement: “not unwelcome”, “no very great”, “not a little”, “rather too much”.

moves.name: Speech reported
moves.does: Speech reported rather than quoted, in the narrator’s syntax: “He said that he was not ready…”.

moves.name: Speech tagged after its first clause
moves.does: Quoted speech that shows character, the speaker named after the first clause, often inverted: “—,” said she, “—.”

moves.name: Feeling shown by conduct
moves.does: Feeling given by its effect on conduct or countenance, not named outright: “she could hardly keep her countenance”, “coloured”.

moves.name: Ironic verdict
moves.does: The narrator’s dry verdict on the situation or on the speaker, implied by precision rather than announced; often a generalization (“It is a truth…”, “as is usual…”) or a deflating last clause.

voices.name: the King James Bible
voices.title: The King James Bible
voices.tagline: And, and, and: the cadence of the Authorized Version

epigraph.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

voices.whole: the whole of the King James Bible

moves.name: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
moves.does: Clause after clause joined by “and”, sentence after sentence opened by it, where English now would subordinate: “And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.”

moves.name: And it came to pass
moves.does: A new turn of the story opened by “And it came to pass”, or closed by “and it was so”.

moves.name: Thou and thee, -eth and -est
moves.does: The singular you as thou, thee, thy, thine, the plural as ye; the verb in -est after thou and in -eth for he and she: “thou knowest”, “he goeth”.

moves.name: Behold, lo, verily
moves.does: Attention called with “behold” or “lo”, an oath with “verily”.

moves.name: Unto, thereof, wherefore
moves.does: The old prepositions and adverbs: unto, upon, thereof, therein, wherefore, whither, thence, hither, yea, nay.

moves.name: Speech brought in by “said unto”
moves.does: Speech introduced plainly, without quotation marks, by “And he said unto them,” and given in full.

moves.name: Parallelism
moves.does: One thought said twice, the second half echoing the first in other words, the halves divided by a colon or semicolon: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.”

moves.name: The genitive with “of”
moves.does: Possession and kind given by “of”: “the house of the LORD”, “the children of Israel”, “the day of his wrath”, not “the LORD’s house”.

voices.name: Abraham Lincoln
voices.title: Abraham Lincoln
voices.tagline: Plain words, a fair premise, the case followed to its end

epigraph.text: If slavery is not wrong, nothing is wrong.
epigraph.cite: Letter to Albert G. Hodges, 4 April 1864

moves.name: The phrase said again
moves.does: The same words open clause after clause, or a phrase comes back with one word changed, so the listener can hold it.

moves.name: Arguing from the premise
moves.does: A condition carried to its end: if this holds, then that must follow.

moves.name: The speaker’s own plain judgement
moves.does: The speaker says what he thinks and what he does not claim: “I think”, “I do not know”, “I have no purpose”.

moves.name: Turning to the listener
moves.does: The speaker turns to the audience and asks them to act together: “let us”, “I ask”, “my friends”.

moves.name: The question put, then answered
moves.does: A question the speaker asks so that he can answer it himself.

moves.name: The term made exact
moves.does: He stops to say exactly what he means: “I mean”, “that is”, “in this sense”.

moves.name: The cases set side by side
moves.does: Each possible case laid out in matching clauses, each with its result; or “not this, but that”.

voices.name: Barack Obama
voices.title: Barack Obama
voices.tagline: Plain talk, one story for many, measured hope

epigraph.text: I am asking you to believe. Not in my ability to bring about change — but in yours.

voices.whole: President Obama’s weekly addresses and speeches

moves.name: From what happened to what we do
moves.does: The turn from the story to its meaning and purpose: “That’s why…”, “And that’s what…”.

moves.name: Not this, but that
moves.does: A claim turned by its opposite: not because it was easy, but because it was right.

moves.name: One American’s story
moves.does: One person, named with a detail, standing for many.

moves.name: Plain talk to the listener
moves.does: The speaker turns to the listener: “Here’s the thing.” “Let me be clear.” “Folks.”

moves.name: The shared “we”
moves.does: What belongs to all of us: together, as a country, who we are.

moves.name: Building in threes
moves.does: Three parallel phrases that build to the point.

voices.name: Mark Twain
voices.title: Mark Twain
voices.tagline: Deadpan, vernacular, the joke at the end

epigraph.text: You don’t know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain’t no matter.

moves.name: Vernacular voice
moves.does: The narrator talks as he would, grammar and all, and the joke is in the voice.

moves.name: Deadpan
moves.does: The absurd stated flatly, the punch line last and never explained.

moves.name: Cumulative sentence
moves.does: A long run of “and … and …” building to a turn.

moves.name: Exaggeration with a straight face
moves.does: An impossible number or comparison stated as plain fact.

moves.name: The narrator’s aside
moves.does: The teller breaks off to comment, confide or correct himself: “I reckon”, “I judge”, “which is”.

samples.title: Book Review: The Lighthouse Year
samples.text:
# Book Review: The Lighthouse Year

The Lighthouse Year is honestly one of the best books I have ever read. I couldn't put it down. I read the whole thing in two days, mostly on the bus and at night when I was supposed to be sleeping.

The characters are amazing and so realistic. The main character is relatable and you really feel what she feels. Her little brother is hilarious. The writing is beautiful and the descriptions make you feel like you're actually there. The plot has so many twists and the ending made me cry.

Some people might say it's slow in the middle, but I didn't think so. It's a coming-of-age story but it's also about family and friendship and growing up.

I would give it five out of five stars. If you like good books, you will love this one. Everyone should read it.

samples.title: Rebuttal: The Four-Day School Week
samples.text:
# Rebuttal: The Four-Day School Week

My opponent says a four-day week would save money and give students more time to rest. But honestly, has my opponent ever actually looked at the numbers? I don't think so. Their whole speech was basically just feelings.

They also said teachers would be happier. Okay, but who cares if teachers are happier if students are falling behind? That's the real issue here. And they talked about a district in another state where it worked, but that's just one district, and things are totally different there.

Also, what are working parents supposed to do on Fridays? My opponent didn't even mention that. That shows they didn't think it through.

Plus, kids would just stay on their phones all day on the extra day off. Everybody knows that's what would happen. So for all these reasons, my opponent's case falls apart, and you should vote for our side.

glossary.definition: Contrary ideas set against each other in balanced words, so each sharpens the other.
glossary.example: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.
glossary.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities

glossary.definition: Saying less than the case warrants, often by denying the opposite, so the reader supplies the rest.
Many conjunctions (“and … and … and”) where commas would do, so each item lands on its own.
glossary.example: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not.

glossary.definition: Clauses of the same length and build set side by side, so the sentence balances.
A group of words with its own subject and verb; a sentence is one clause or several joined.
